title: When algorithms cannot be fair: constitutive and contingent discrimination and the limits of less-discriminatory alternatives
abstract: Abstract The literature on algorithmic fairness has concentrated on the choice amongst fairness metrics, a choice constrained by well-known impossibility results (Chouldechova 2017; Kleinberg et al. 2017). This paper argues that a prior question deserves equal attention: how the categories, variables, and objective functions that constitute an algorithmic system’s representation of its domain are chosen, and when those choices themselves discriminate? We propose a criterion for distinguishing two kinds of algorithmic discrimination. A disparity is contingent, relative to a legitimate purpose and a class of admissible designs, when an alternative design within that class serves the purpose whilst reducing the disparity; it is constitutive, relative to the same parameters, when no such alternative is available. Because contingency is an existential claim and constitutivity a negative existential over a class of designs, the two carry asymmetric obligations: contingency is shown by exhibit, constitutivity by documented exhaustion, and neither is discharged by assertion. Every constitutivity claim therefore states in advance the exhibit that would refute it, which is what makes the distinction actionable in design review, audit, and litigation rather than merely classificatory. The criterion adapts the comparative logic of the less-discriminatory alternative from disparate-impact doctrine (Laufer et al. 2025) and shifts it from the level of models and outcomes to the level of representational choices, whose distinctive rigidity we analyse through the notion of open texture (Waismann 1945; Hart 1961): computational systems fix ex ante the precisifications that human decision-makers perform case by case. Three case studies (the ImageNet person categories, tokeniser-level disparities in large language models, and automated hiring together with clinical risk scoring) are used to test, not merely to illustrate, the criterion. We conclude by proposing ontological auditing, an upstream evaluation of representational choices articulated through an Ontological Impact Statement, and by locating it within the risk management and data governance provisions of the EU AI Act.

claims.text: Computational systems fix the precisification of open-textured concepts ex ante, uniformly, and at scale during design time.

An algorithmic disparity is contingent relative to a legitimate purpose, a disparity measure, and an admissible class of operationalisations if an alternative operationalisation in that class serves the purpose while reducing the disparity.

An algorithmic disparity is constitutive relative to a legitimate purpose, a disparity measure, and an admissible class of operationalisations if no alternative operationalisation in that class supports such a system.
Contingency claims carry an epistemic burden of exhibition, requiring the production of an admissible alternative operationalisation.
Constitutivity claims carry an epistemic burden of documented exhaustion over the class of admissible designs and remain defeasible by a single counterexample.
The disparity produced by derogatory person categories in ImageNet inherited from WordNet was contingent relative to the purpose of benchmarking object recognition.
Character-level and byte-level encodings still exhibit more than a fourfold difference in encoding length for certain language pairs.
Re-operationalising health need through measures of health rather than healthcare cost reduced racial disparity in the clinical risk algorithm by 84%.
Fairness impossibility theorems are a limiting case of constitutive discrimination relative to a design class that holds population partitions and base rates fixed.

limitations.text: The criterion provides no theory for normatively fixing the legitimate purpose, disparity measure, or admissible design space parameters.

Operationalising the representational LDA test depends heavily on adequate held-out data and is constrained by the resource costs of developing candidate operationalisations sufficiently to evaluate them.
The analyzed case studies are illustrative and selected adversarially rather than representing a statistically representative sample of deployed algorithmic systems.
The paper's own analytical distinctions coarsen and simplify the complex representational practices they seek to organize.
The proposed Ontological Impact Statement and sociotechnical review committees are untested in institutional practice, and their administrative costs remain unknown.

future_work.text: Formalize the criterion as a mathematical theory of comparative information loss across admissible design spaces to derive formal necessary conditions for constitutivity.
Investigate methods for delimiting admissible design classes, specifically differentiating classes constrained by technical necessity from those bounded by commercial conventions.
Trial the Ontological Impact Statement in real-world design processes to assess its practical feasibility and administrative burden.

methodologies.name: Representational Less-Discriminatory Alternative (LDA) Test Protocol
methodologies.description: A four-step analytical protocol to evaluate whether algorithmic disparities are contingent or constitutive relative to a specified purpose, disparity measure, and admissible design space.
conditions: Explicitly bounded class of admissible operationalisations C

methodologies.name: Ontological Auditing via Ontological Impact Statement
methodologies.description: An upstream audit mechanism documenting construct representations, excluded dimensions, proxy relationships, considered alternatives, and justifications of constitutivity claims before system deployment.
conditions: Conducted upstream during design prior to finalising data collection and architecture
